### Problem: Subarray Product Less Than K {#sec-sw-p4-a}

::: {.p-statement}
An array `nums` of $n$ **positive** integers ($1 \le n \le 3\cdot10^4$, $1 \le \mathit{nums}[i] \le 1000$) and an integer $k$ ($0 \le k \le 10^6$). Count the contiguous subarrays whose product is **strictly less than** $k$.

Source: [LC 713 · Subarray Product Less Than K](https://leetcode.com/problems/subarray-product-less-than-k/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Count, don't maximise. For a fixed right end `r`, all subarrays ending at `r` are `nums[i..r]` for $i = 0..r$; their products only *grow* as $i$ moves left (positivity). So the valid ones form a **suffix** of that list: from some `l` up to `r`. Maintain the window product and shrink `l` while the product reaches $k$; when it stops, every start in `l..r` is valid and there are exactly $r - l + 1$ of them. Add that count each step. This is the "count all subarrays ending at `r`" trick of @sec-sw-a4.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Enumerate subarrays.** Double loop multiplying out each product, count those $< k$, breaking as soon as one reaches $k$ (positivity: everything further right only grows). $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ space — the oracle.
2. **Fix the left end, chase the right.** For each start $l$, extend a running product until the next factor would reach $k$; that stop point bounds *all* of $l$'s valid subarrays at once, so add $r - l + 1$ and move on. Still $O(n^2)$ multiplications in the worst case (all ones), $O(1)$ space — the boundary is recomputed from scratch per left end, missing that the stop point for $l+1$ is never left of the stop point for $l$.
3. **Window + $r - l + 1$ per right end.** Grow `r` into `prod`; while `prod >= k` divide out `nums[l]`. Add `r - l + 1`. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space — one shared boundary for all right ends, the batch trick of @sec-sw-a4.

**Invariant.** After the inner `while`, `prod` $= \prod_{i=l}^{r} \mathit{nums}[i] < k$, and $l$ is the **smallest** left index with that property (positivity: every start left of $l$ gives a product $\ge k$), so exactly the $r - l + 1$ windows `nums[l..r], nums[l+1..r], \dots, nums[r..r]` are the valid subarrays ending at $r$.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Enumerate every subarray

::: {.form-next}
Two loops, multiply each product, count. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ space — the oracle.

**"Product less than $k$", in plain words.** Multiply every contiguous stretch of `nums` and count the stretches whose product comes out strictly below $k$. Because all values are positive, extending a stretch multiplies in a factor $\ge 1$, so the product can only grow — which is why, for a fixed start, we can `break` the moment the product reaches $k$: nothing further right will ever be small enough again.

**Worked example.** nums $= [10, 5, 2, 6]$, $k = 100$. Starting at $10$: $[10]$ (product $10 < 100$, count), $[10, 5]$ ($50 < 100$, count), but $[10, 5, 2]$ ($100$, *not* strictly below) so stop. Starting at $5$: $[5]$, $[5, 2]$, $[5, 2, 6]$ all clear. Starting at $2$: $[2]$, $[2, 6]$. Starting at $6$: $[6]$. That is $2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 8$ subarrays. (A common slip is to keep $[10, 5, 2]$, but its product is exactly $100$, which fails the *strictly less than* test.)
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def count_prod_brute(nums, k):
    n, cnt = len(nums), 0
    for i in range(n):
        p = 1
        for j in range(i, n):
            p *= nums[j]
            if p < k:
                cnt += 1
            else:
                break
    return cnt
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - brute force oracle
#include <vector>
using namespace std;
int countProductBrute(const vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    int n = (int)nums.size(), cnt = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        long long p = 1;
        for (int j = i; j < n; ++j) {
            p *= nums[j];
            if (p < k) ++cnt; else break;
        }
    }
    return cnt;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The outer loop fixes the start `i`; `p = 1` resets an empty product for that start. The inner loop does `p *= nums[j]` to extend one element rightward; `if p < k` counts this stretch (`cnt += 1`), and `else: break` stops extending because positive factors mean every longer stretch from `i` has an even bigger product. Returning `cnt` simply reports every stretch the double loop found under $k$.

#### Fix the left end, chase the furthest right

::: {.form-next}
Count per *start* instead of per end: run a product rightwards from $l$ until the next factor would reach $k$, then everything from `nums[l..l]` up to `nums[l..r]` is valid — bank $r - l + 1$ and reset for $l+1$. $O(n^2)$ time in the worst case (all ones: every start runs to the end), $O(1)$ space — it lacks only the *sharing* the window exploits.

**Count many subarrays with one number.** Fixing the start $l$, we push a running product rightward until adding one more factor would reach $k$. Say it stops at end $r$: then `nums[l..l]`, `nums[l..l+1]`, …, `nums[l..r]` are *all* valid at once, which is exactly $r - l + 1$ subarrays — so we bank that whole count in one step instead of tallying each. It's a per-start version of the same "products only grow" idea from form 1's worked example.

**Worked example.** nums $= [10, 5, 2, 6]$, $k = 100$. From $l = 0$ (value $10$) we can extend to $[10, 5]$ (product $50$) but not $[10, 5, 2]$ ($100$), so the furthest end is $r = 1$ and we bank $r - l + 1 = 2$ subarrays. From $l = 1$ we reach $r = 3$ and bank $3$, and so on; the per-start banks sum to $8$.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-713-perleft
def count_prod_perleft(nums, k):
    n, cnt = len(nums), 0
    for l in range(n):
        p, r = 1, l - 1
        while r + 1 < n and p * nums[r + 1] < k:   # chase the furthest valid right end
            p *= nums[r + 1]
            r += 1
        cnt += r - l + 1                           # every end from l..r is valid
    return cnt

for _ in range(300):
    nums = [random.randint(1, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 10))]
    k = random.randint(2, 60)
    assert count_prod_perleft(nums, k) == count_prod_brute(nums, k)
assert count_prod_perleft([10, 5, 2, 6], 100) == 8                  # LC example
print("count_prod_perleft OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int numSubarrayProductLessThanKPerLeft(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    int n = (int)nums.size(); long long cnt = 0;
    for (int l = 0; l < n; ++l) {
        long long p = 1; int r = l - 1;
        while (r + 1 < n && p * nums[r + 1] < k) p *= nums[++r];
        cnt += r - l + 1;
    }
    return (int)cnt;
}

int main() { vector<int> v{10,5,2,6}; numSubarrayProductLessThanKPerLeft(v, 100); }
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** For each start `l`, `p, r = 1, l - 1` opens an empty product positioned just before the start. The `while r + 1 < n and p * nums[r + 1] < k` test peeks one step ahead — it only commits the multiply (`p *= nums[r + 1]`) and advances `r` when the *next* factor keeps the product strictly under $k$. When the loop stops, every end from `l` through `r` is valid, so `cnt += r - l + 1` banks them in bulk. The boundary is rebuilt from scratch for each `l` — the next form shows how to *carry* it instead.

#### Count $r - l + 1$ at each right end

::: {.form-next}
Keep the window product under $k$; the number of valid subarrays ending at `r` is just the window length. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space — and unlike the per-left chase, the boundary is *carried*: `l` never rewinds, so the whole count is one shared sweep.

**The sliding window, in plain words (this chapter's new tool).** Keep *one* window `nums[l..r]` whose product `prod` is always under $k$. Grow by multiplying in the element at `r`; if `prod` reaches $k$, divide elements out of the left until it fits again. When it settles, every start from `l` to `r` gives a valid subarray ending at `r` — that's $r - l + 1$ of them — so we add the current window *length* each step. Because `l` only ever moves forward, both pointers sweep the array once, giving $O(n)$.

**Worked example.** nums $= [10, 5, 2, 6]$, $k = 100$. $r = 0$: $\mathit{prod} = 10$, add $1$. $r = 1$: $\mathit{prod} = 50$, add $2$ (windows $[5], [10, 5]$). $r = 2$: $\mathit{prod} = 100 \ge 100$, so divide out $10 \to 10$ with $l = 1$, add $2$ ($[2], [5, 2]$). $r = 3$: $\mathit{prod} = 60$, add $3$ ($[6], [2, 6], [5, 2, 6]$). Total $1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8$.
:::

```{python}

    assert str(final) == "8"

V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-713-count
def count_product(nums, k):
    l = 0
    prod = 1
    cnt = 0
    for r, x in enumerate(nums):
        prod *= x                           # grow the window product
        while prod >= k and l <= r:         # shrink until strictly under k
            prod //= nums[l]
            l += 1
        cnt += r - l + 1                     # every start in [l..r] is valid
    return cnt

for _ in range(300):
    nums = [random.randint(1, 12) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 12))]
    k = random.randint(1, 60)
    assert count_product(nums, k) == count_prod_brute(nums, k)
assert count_product([10, 5, 2, 6], 100) == 8               # LC example, and the board sample
assert count_product([1, 2, 3], 0) == 0                     # k=0 -> none
assert count_product([1, 1, 1], 2) == 6                     # all-ones windows
print("count_product OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int numSubarrayProductLessThanK(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    if (k <= 0) return 0;
    long long prod = 1;
    int l = 0, cnt = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < (int)nums.size(); ++r) {
        prod *= nums[r];
        while (prod >= k && l <= r) { prod /= nums[l]; ++l; }
        cnt += r - l + 1;
    }
    return cnt;
}

int main() { vector<int> v{10,5,2,6}; numSubarrayProductLessThanK(v, 100); }
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `l = 0`, `prod = 1`, `cnt = 0` open an empty window, its product, and the running count. `for r, x in enumerate(nums)` brings the new right element in via `prod *= x`. `while prod >= k and l <= r` shrinks from the front — `prod //= nums[l]` divides it out and `l += 1` advances — until the window product is strictly under $k$ again; the `l <= r` guard handles a single element already $\ge k$ (window empties). `cnt += r - l + 1` then adds every valid subarray ending at `r` in one line, because they are exactly the window's $r - l + 1$ suffixes. Each pointer moves only forward, so the whole sweep is $O(n)$.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Enumerate every subarray** is $O(n^2)$ time worst case (many small products), $O(1)$ space. **Fix the left end** is $O(n^2)$ time in the worst case (products that stay tiny, such as all ones), $O(1)$ space — the same ceiling as the brute force, just batched per start. **Window + count** is $O(n)$: `prod` grows once per `r` and is divided at most $n$ times overall, so the loop is linear; the answer is at most $\binom{n+1}{2} \approx 4.5\cdot10^8$ for $n = 3\cdot10^4$, which fits a 32-bit `int` — but only just within a factor of five, so a 64-bit counter is the safe habit (@sec-arr-cost). `prod` is kept $< k \le 10^6$ before each multiply, so it stays within $10^9$ — `long long` removes any doubt.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $k \le 1$: no positive product is $< 1$, and the `while` empties the window every step (the `l <= r` guard stops it there), so `cnt` stays $0$. The C++ adds an explicit `k <= 0` guard for clarity.
- Ones everywhere (`nums=[1,1,1], k=2`): every subarray is valid; the window never shrinks and $\sum (r-l+1) = \binom{n+1}{2} = 6$.
- **Positivity is essential**: `prod //= nums[l]` only undoes the multiply when `nums[l] != 0`, and products are monotone in the window only for positive factors; a $0$ or a negative value breaks the whole "smallest valid `l`" argument (@sec-sw-a5).
:::

::: {.practice}
- [LC 2302 · Count Subarrays With Score Less Than K](https://leetcode.com/problems/count-subarrays-with-score-less-than-k/){difficulty="Hard"} — the score is sum times length, still monotone under shrinking, so the same `r - l + 1` batch counts it.
- [CF 1736C1 · Good Subarrays (Easy Version)](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1736/C1){rating="1300"} — the rule depends on the position inside the window, but it is still monotone, so `l` only moves forward.
:::
